title: How Data Shapes a Solution's Outcome
summary: Students trace how the examples a fruit-ripeness sorter learned from decide the answer it gives, then predict how changing that data would move the outcome.
objectives: Explain how the data used changes the outcome of a given solution.
Predict how a change in the data would change the solution's result.

body: Two apps can share the exact same code and still disagree about the same photo. The secret is not in the code it is in what each app was shown. Today you become a data detective, tracing how the examples an app learns from decide the answer it gives.

sections.heading: I can…
items: I can explain, in my own words, how the data fed into a solution shapes the outcome it produces.
I can predict what would happen to the outcome if the data were changed, and give a reason.
I can point to a specific part of the data that most affects the result.

terms.definition: The whole system that solves a problem - the data plus the model built from it.
The examples a solution learns from.
The answer or result the solution gives.
The regularity a model finds across many examples.
Whether the data has roughly fair amounts of each category.

sections.heading: A solution is data plus a model
body: When people say an app 'decides', they often picture a programmer writing every rule by hand. Machine-learning solutions do not work that way. They build a **model** by studying [[data]] - lots of examples - and capturing the [[pattern]]s inside.

Because the pattern comes from the examples, the examples quietly control the answer. Feed the model different data and it learns a different pattern, so it gives a different [[outcome]], even with the very same code.

sections.label: What a solution is made of
sections.heading: Data plus a model
sections.altText: A bar split into two parts — the data and the model — which together produce the outcome.

parts.label: The model
parts.detail: the pattern it found in them

sections.caption: Change the data and the outcome changes, even with the same model. **That is why tracing a bad outcome starts at the data**, not at the answer.

sections.heading: Amount and balance both matter
body: Data influences an outcome in two ways. First, the *amount*: if the model saw 100 sunny photos and only 3 rainy ones, it treats sunny as normal and stumbles on rain.

Second, the [[balance]]: adding more of what the model already has plenty of changes little, but adding examples of a rare or missing category can move the outcome a lot. A data detective looks for the gap.

sections.label: Hands-on
sections.heading: Let's try it - hands-on
body: Your teacher will run a fruit-ripeness sorter on the board. Your job is not to run it - it is to trace why it answers the way it does, using the data list on your card.
items: Read the data list on your card and say what the sorter mostly saw.
Watch one fruit go through and note the outcome.
Draw an arrow from the data batch you think caused that outcome.
Write: 'The outcome is ___ because the data mostly showed ___.'
Check your reason against a second fruit - does the story still hold?

sections.heading: Think about it
items: Which data batch had the biggest effect on the outcome, and how do you know?
If you could add only one batch of new data, which would you add to make the sorter fairer?

sections.heading: My reflection
items: Write one sentence explaining how data shaped today's outcome.
Note one thing you would check before trusting a solution's answer.

worksheet.title: Week 3 - Core - Worksheet | How Data Shapes a Solution's Outcome

questions.prompt: Two date-sorting apps run exactly the same code. Shown the same photo of a brown date, one app answers 'ripe' and the other answers 'unripe'. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The two apps learned from different sets of example photos, so each one found a different pattern.
One app's code must contain a mistake, because identical code always has to give identical answers.
One app is guessing, because apps answer at random whenever a photo is hard to judge.
The apps were given the same examples, but one of them studied the photo for longer.

feedback.correct: Right - the code is only half of a solution; the examples it learned from decide the pattern, and the pattern decides the outcome.
feedback.incorrect: Identical code can still disagree: each app built its model from different examples, so each learned a different pattern and gives a different outcome.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in order to show how the data ends up shaping the sorter's answer about a new date.

items.text: The model captures the pattern it keeps seeing across those examples.
Photos of dates, each labelled ripe or unripe, are collected as the data.
The sorter gives an outcome for a new date it has never seen.
The model studies the collected examples.

feedback.correct: Exactly - the data comes first, the pattern comes from the data, and the outcome comes from the pattern.
feedback.incorrect: The chain runs data first: examples are collected, the model studies them, it captures a pattern, and only then can it give an outcome for a new date.

questions.prompt: A sorter learned from 200 photos of brown ripe dates and only 5 photos of green unripe dates. Select ALL the changes that would move its outcomes a lot.

options.text: Adding 60 photos of green unripe dates.
Adding 60 more photos of brown ripe dates.
Adding 60 photos of half-ripe yellow dates, a colour it has never been shown.
Removing 3 of the 200 brown ripe photos.
Running the same 200 brown ripe photos through the model a second time.

feedback.correct: Yes - the green and yellow batches fill gaps in categories the sorter barely had, and gaps are where the outcome moves most.
feedback.incorrect: Adding, removing or repeating brown photos only reinforces a pattern the sorter already has; it is the missing or rare categories, green and yellow, that shift the outcome.

questions.prompt: True or false: for a sorter that already learned from 200 brown ripe dates, adding 100 more brown ripe photos will change its outcomes more than adding 20 green unripe photos would.

feedback.correct: Correct - size alone does not decide influence; 20 photos of a category the sorter is missing shift the outcome more than 100 more of what it already has.
feedback.incorrect: It is false: the 100 extra brown photos repeat a pattern the sorter already learned, while the 20 green photos fill a gap, and filling a gap moves the outcome far more.

questions.prompt: The sorter learned from 200 brown ripe dates and 5 green unripe dates. Match each change to the outcome you should predict from it.

left.text: Add 50 photos of green dates labelled 'unripe'.
Add 50 more photos of brown dates labelled 'ripe'.
Change nothing in the data, but let a different class use the app.

right.text: The sorter starts calling green dates 'unripe' - a big shift, because a missing category has been filled.
The outcome barely moves, because the new examples repeat a pattern the sorter already had plenty of.
The outcome stays exactly the same, because it comes from the data and the model, not from who is using the app.

feedback.correct: Well matched - you predicted each outcome from what the data gained, which is exactly how a data detective reasons.
feedback.incorrect: Predict from the gap: new examples of a missing category move the outcome, more of the same barely does, and changing the user changes nothing at all.

formative.targets: Grade 4 Advanced: explains how data influences the outcome of a solution
formative.check: Data-to-outcome explanation on a worked solution (with a 'what if the data changed' probe)
formative.successCriteria: Correctly explains the data's influence and predicts the effect of a data change.
